name: Transaction Validation
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: Why the Network Doesn't Just Take Your Word For It
lesson.summary: Transaction validation is the process by which nodes check that a submitted transaction follows the network's rules, most importantly that it carries a genuine digital signature and does not spend value the sender does not actually have, before it is allowed into a block.
lesson.body:
A transaction, as described in the previous section, is just a claim: "I am sending this amount to this address." Nothing about writing that claim down makes it true. Transaction validation is the process that stands between a submitted transaction and its acceptance into the ledger, and it is what prevents a blockchain from being a system where anyone can simply announce they own something and have the network believe them.

The most fundamental check draws directly on digital signatures, covered earlier in this course. Every transaction must be signed with the private key corresponding to the sender's public address, and any node receiving the transaction can verify that signature using only the sender's public key and the transaction's contents, without ever needing to know the private key itself. If the signature does not verify, meaning it was not produced by the claimed sender's private key, the transaction is rejected outright, no different in principle from a bank refusing a check with a forged signature, except the verification here is mathematical rather than a human comparing handwriting.

Beyond authenticity, nodes check consistency with the ledger's actual history. This is where the transaction concept from the previous section connects back to earlier material on distributed ledgers and immutability: a node checks whether the sender genuinely has the funds or state being spent, by consulting the accumulated, tamper evident record of prior transactions. Attempting to spend the same funds twice, known as a double spend, is rejected because a node checking the ledger's history can see the funds were already spent, or, on networks using unspent output accounting, that the specific output being referenced no longer exists. This is a big part of why the earlier immutability discussion matters practically and not just philosophically: validation is only meaningful if the history being checked against cannot be quietly altered.

A worked example: imagine Priya, from the earlier transaction example, tries to send the same 2 units to both Jamal and a third person, Wei, using two separate transactions that reference the same source funds, submitted to the network within moments of each other. Nodes receiving both transactions will validate each one's signature successfully, since both are genuinely signed by Priya. But they cannot validate both as spending the same funds. Depending on which transaction a given node saw first, or which one ultimately gets included in a block by whoever assembles it, one transaction succeeds and the other is rejected as invalid once the network converges on a single accepted history. This is precisely the kind of conflict that consensus mechanisms, covered elsewhere in this course, exist to resolve consistently across the whole network.

It is worth being precise about what validation does and does not guarantee. Validation confirms a transaction was authorized by the claimed sender and does not violate the ledger's accounting rules. It says nothing about whether the transaction was a good idea, whether the sender was scammed into signing it, or whether the recipient is trustworthy. A perfectly valid transaction can still send funds to a thief, because validity is a statement about mathematical and procedural correctness, not about wisdom or intent.
